newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: China goes on with pak nuclear cooperation.
newsitem.headline: China goes on with pak nuclear cooperation.

text.p: China vowed on Sunday to continue peaceful nuclear cooperation with Pakistan but said it had not transferred nuclear technology for military purposes to Islamabad.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin discussed the issue with his Pakistani counterpart Farooq Leghari in talks after arriving for a four-day visit, a Chinese spokesman said.

China and Pakistan enjoy good cooperation in the utilisation of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes which is strictlty supervised by the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency)...and our cooperation in this regard will continue," he told reporters.
Jiang earlier arrived to a warm welcome on the second leg of a regional tour, which Pakistani analysts said held out a hope of helping to ease tensions on the fractious sub-continent.

U.S.-made F-16 fighters of the Pakistan Air Force escorted Jiang's Boeing 747-400 plane as he flew in from India, Pakistan's arch rival, where the two asian giants signed an agreement aimed at reducing tensions along their Himalayan border, site of a brief border war in 1962.
The Chinese spokesman, Shen Guofang, quoted Leghari as telling Jiang in their 90-minute meeting that Pakistan had no fears from the new warmth between Beijing and New Delhi.
President Leghari believes that the improvement and development of relations between China and India will not adversely affect the relations between China and Pakistan.
He said the two sides had reached very important common understanding in terms of political relations and also discussed ways to promote economic cooperation and trade.
Jiang later said in a speech that Beijing was ready to carry close ties with Islamabad into the 21st century.
"History has proven and will continue to prove that China and Pakistan are true friends in need who have stood together through thick and thin," he said in the speech at a banquet given by Leghari.

"We are ready to work together with our Pakistani friends from all walks of life and encourage each other in our efforts to build all round cooperative partnership between China and Pakistan for the 21st century."
Analysts in Pakistan, whose ties with Beijing have been close for 30 years, welcomed China's pact with India, saying good relations between them should benefit the whole region.

"It has been proved that China-Pakistan friendship not only conforms to the fundamental interests of the two countries and peoples, but also contributes to the maintenance of peace and stability of South Asia and Asia at large," Jiang said in a prepared arrival statement.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947 and Islamabad has leaned heavily on Chinese support.

New Delhi believes that includes supplies of missiles and nuclear technology, which Islamabad and Beijing deny. India, which denies having built atomic bombs despite setting off a nuclear explosion in 1974, has its own missile programme.
Jiang leaves on wednesday for Nepal, the third and last stop on his regional tour.
